QF.id: XIII Introduction to the Underlying Markets_64

question.text: If the risk-free rate for India is 7% and for the US is 3%, what does interest rate parity suggest about the one-year USDINR forward rate if the spot is Rs 83?

answer.text: The one-year forward rate should be higher than Rs 83 (INR at a forward discount) because Indian interest rates are higher than US rates
The forward rate should be lower than Rs 83 (INR at a forward premium)
The forward rate should be exactly Rs 83 (no change from spot)
Interest rate parity does not apply to the USDINR pair

explanation.text: The Logic: Under interest rate parity, F = S × (1 + R_QC × period) / (1 + R_BC × period), where QC is the quote currency (INR) and BC is the base currency (USD). For a one-year tenor with R_INR = 7% and R_USD = 3%, the USDINR forward is above the spot of Rs 83, so the INR trades at a forward discount. The Trap: A common misconception is that the higher-yielding currency must strengthen in the forward market; IRP shows the opposite — the currency with the higher interest rate quotes at a forward discount. Note: Any persistent deviation from this IRP relationship would create covered-interest-arbitrage opportunities, which is why traded forward rates tend to track the formula closely.
